To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the antibiotic resister clones emerging de novo in vitro from the surviving population of Mycobacteriaceae and other bacterial species, which have been reported in our laboratory and in others' laboratories, multiply using a unique cell division mechanism involving multinucleation and multiple constrictions.

the antibiotic genetic resister cells formed de novo in the presence of rifampicins/moxifloxacins become multinucleated and multi-septated and develop multiple constrictions to produce multiple daughter cells.

the rifampicinsurviving mycobacterial population generated elevated levels and increased persistence of hydroxyl radicals, which inflicted mutations in the population and selected against the antibiotic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism by which the antibiotic genetic resister bacteria formed de novo multiply to establish an antibiotic-resistant population and how the same can be preempted.
the mechanisms of emergence of antibiotic resisters of bacterial pathogens.
the mechanism of emergence of antibiotic genetic resistance in bacterial species, which is of global importance in public health and clinical medicine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study unraveled the unique mode of bacterial cell division by the antibiotic resister clones emerging de novo from the surviving population in the continued presence antibiotics.

this study unravels an important phenomenon that is not only significant to the understanding of the emergence of bacterial genetic resisters but is also important in the design of strategies to combat the emergence of bacterial resistance to the existing antibiotics.

the antibiotic genetic resister cells formed de novo in the continued presence and exposure to the antibiotic are multinucleated, multiseptated, and develop multiple constrictions, which allow them to divide multiple times and stochastically produce a higher number of sister daughter cells than what could be predicted from their growth characteristics, thus establishing an antibiotic resister bacterial population abruptly and unexpectedly.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the antibiotic resisters of Myco. and others' bacteria formed de novo in the presence of antibiotics use a unique mode of cell multiplication for quick multiplication to generate a large antibiotic resister population.
the present study provides the cellular mechanism for the emergence and establishment of antibiotic genetic resister populations.

the antibiotic genetic resister bacillary clones, once emerged, might use this unique mechanism to multiply and establish an antibiotic resistant bacterial population quickly in the presence of antibiotics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bacterial pathogens that are surviving in the presence antibiotics have the chance for acquiring genetic mutations against the antibiotics.

the bacterial antibiotic resisters formed de novo from antibiotic surviving bacterial populations are not only resistant but multiply quickly and establish antibiotic resistant populations in the presence of antibiotics, which is the main cause of antibiotic resistance.

the bacterial pathogens that are resistant to antibiotics and survive against antibiotics have a chance to acquire genetic mutations against the antibiotics, and the genetic mutations can emerge de novo from the antibiotic surviving population as antibiotic resisters, and the antibiotic resister clones can use the unique cell division mode to establish a population in the continued presence/absence of the antibiotics.
